subject: social_science
chapter_title: The Making of a Global World: Trade, Migration and Depression

concepts.title: Silk Routes Linking the World
concepts.definition: Pre-modern trade and cultural exchange flowed along silk routes, a web of land and sea paths that carried west-bound Chinese silk cargoes alongside pottery, textiles, spices, metals and religious ideas between Asia, Europe and North Africa.
concepts.key_idea: Christian missionaries and Muslim preachers travelled these routes centuries ago, proving that goods and beliefs moved together across continents.
question_patterns: what is the significance of the silk routes
which goods travelled along the silk routes
how did the silk routes link asia with europe and north africa
what ideas spread through pre modern trade routes
why are silk routes important in the history of globalisation
name the goods and religions that moved on the silk routes

solution_steps.explain: Distinguish the multiple land and sea silk routes that knit together Asia, Europe and North Africa.
Chinese silk led the cargoes; pottery, textiles and spices followed, while Chinese pottery also travelled the same paths.
Confirm that missionaries and preachers used the same routes, carrying Christian and Muslim teachings along with merchandise.

concepts.title: Food Travels and the Columbian Exchange
concepts.definition: Everyday foods crossed continents long ago, and after Christopher Columbus's voyages the Americas gave potatoes, maize, chillies, tomatoes and sweet potatoes to the world, transforming diets everywhere.
concepts.key_idea: Noodles and spaghetti are argued to have travelled from China and Arabia to Italy, showing that trade routes moved recipes as surely as merchandise.
question_patterns: which foods spread from the americas to the rest of the world
how did noodles and spaghetti travel across continents
what is meant by food travels in global history
what role did christopher columbus play in food exchange
how did common foods like potatoes and chillies reach asia and europe
explain the columbian exchange with examples of crops

solution_steps.explain: Place each food in its homeland, such as American crops like potato, maize and tomato before Columbus.
Match traders and travellers, from silk route carriers to Columbus's voyages, that moved the crops and dishes.
Check how new staples changed cuisines, as spaghetti in Italy and potatoes in Asia show.

concepts.title: Conquest, Disease and Trade after Columbus
concepts.definition: European conquest of the Americas succeeded less by guns than by germs, since smallpox carried across the Atlantic killed entire communities and cleared the way for colonisation and the global silver trade.
concepts.key_idea: Until the nineteenth century, poverty and hunger were common in Europe, and the search for food and precious metals drove long-distance commerce.
question_patterns: why is smallpox called a powerful ally of the spanish conquerors
how did disease help european conquest of the americas
what role did silver mines of peru and mexico play in world trade
why did europeans search for sea routes to asia
how did the global silver trade work
what was the condition of europe before the nineteenth century

solution_steps.explain: Recognise that smallpox proved the deadliest tool, wiping out native communities before armies fought.
Trace silver from American mines through Europe to Asia in exchange for silk, spices and other goods.
Note European poverty and hunger as the pressure that pushed expansion and trade in goods.

concepts.title: The Nineteenth Century World Economy
concepts.definition: Between 1815 and 1914 a world economy took shape as technology, capital and migration moved together: railways and canals linked farmlands to ports, and roughly 150 million people emigrated from Europe to work in the Americas and Australia.
concepts.key_idea: Canal Colonies irrigated by new canals in Punjab turned wasteland into wheat export zones, while corn law abolition in Britain opened food markets to the world.
question_patterns: how did technology transform the nineteenth century world economy
what were canal colonies and where were they set up
why were the corn laws abolished in britain
which regions fed the growing industrial cities of europe
how did migration shape the nineteenth century global economy
describe the movement of capital goods and workers across the world

solution_steps.explain: Trade in goods, flows of capital and movement of people together built the nineteenth century economy.
Railways, steamships and canals cut transport costs, letting grain from America and Australia reach Europe.
Check examples like Punjab's Canal Colonies turning new irrigation land into export wheat fields.

concepts.title: Rinderpest and the Conquest of Africa
concepts.definition: Rinderpest, a devastating cattle disease, arrived in Africa in the late 1880s and wiped out two-thirds of the cattle, destroying African livelihoods and easing European seizure of land and labour for plantations and mines.
concepts.key_idea: The loss of cattle forced Africans to work for wages, so a virus deepened colonial control of the continent.
question_patterns: how did rinderpest help the european conquest of africa
what was rinderpest and how did it reach africa
what effect did the cattle plague have on african livelihoods
why were europeans attracted to africa in the late nineteenth century
how did loss of cattle force africans into wage labour
explain the link between disease and colonisation in africa

solution_steps.explain: Rinderpest entered through East Africa in the late 1880s, carried with imported cattle, and spread westwards.
The plague killed most cattle, on which African livelihoods and self-sufficiency depended.
Confirm that desperate Africans were pushed into working for settlers and mine owners, converting disease into labour control.

concepts.title: Indentured Labour Migration from India
concepts.definition: In the nineteenth century hundreds of thousands of Indian labourers signed contracts of indenture to work on plantations, in mines and in construction across the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji, Malaya and Ceylon, under a bonded system of harsh conditions.
concepts.key_idea: Recruits came largely from the districts of eastern Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and central India, and songs and memoirs of the workers kept alive the memory of hardship in the sugar and tea colonies.
question_patterns: describe the indentured labour migration from india
where did indian indentured workers go and why
what does the term indentured labour mean
how were indentured workers recruited and treated
which regions supplied the indentured labourers
what was the legacy of the indenture system

solution_steps.explain: An indentured labourer is a bonded worker bound by a contract for a fixed period under hard conditions.
Caribbean islands like Trinidad, Mauritius, Fiji, Malaya and Ceylon received workers drawn from eastern and central India.
Note the hardships recalled in songs and the rise of Indo-Caribbean and Indo-Fijian communities of famous descendants.

concepts.title: British Manufactures and the Indian Economy
concepts.definition: From the early nineteenth century British machine-made manufactures flooded Indian markets, while India became an exporter of raw materials and foodstuffs and a huge consumer of British goods, tightening its colonial role in the world economy.
concepts.key_idea: Indian handicrafts collapsed under imported cloth, and in the reverse direction Britain used India's export surplus to balance its own trade deficits.
question_patterns: how did british manufactures affect indian handicrafts
why did india export raw materials to britain
what was the role of india's export surplus in the world economy
how did the british control indian trade
describe the changes in india's foreign trade in the nineteenth century
why is india called a colony in the world economy

solution_steps.explain: India exported raw cotton and food grains and imported finished British manufactures.
Machine-made cloth undercut weavers, pushing artisans into agriculture.
Britain financed its deficits and war costs by drawing on India's export surplus through 'home charges'.

concepts.title: The Great Depression and Its Indian Impact
concepts.definition: The Great Depression that began around 1929 brought catastrophic declines in production, employment and incomes worldwide, and in India wheat prices fell by 50 per cent between 1928 and 1934 while jute prices collapsed by 60 per cent, driving peasants deeper into debt.
concepts.key_idea: Agricultural prices fell more sharply than industrial prices, so colonial farmers lost income while urban dwellers with fixed incomes actually gained from cheap goods.
question_patterns: what were the effects of the great depression on india
how much did wheat prices fall in india between 1928 and 1934
why did the great depression hurt peasants more than landlords
describe the causes of the great depression
how did the depression spread from the united states to the world
which sections of indian society gained from falling prices

solution_steps.explain: Follow the chain from US farm overproduction and bank failures through world trade to colonial economies.
Wheat prices fell 50 per cent from 1928 to 1934; jute growers saw prices drop by 60 per cent, deepening rural debt.
Peasants and workers suffered collapsing incomes while fixed-income town dwellers found goods cheaper.

concepts.title: Wheat Price Fall in Per Cent
concepts.definition: A price fall expressed in per cent converts to an actual drop by multiplying the earlier price by the fall percentage, as with Indian wheat whose price halved during the depression years.
concepts.key_idea: Between 1928 and 1934 Indian wheat prices fell 50 per cent and jute prices 60 per cent, so a grower selling at a quarter of the earlier price is consistent with such collapses.
question_patterns: calculate the fall in wheat price given the percentage decline
how many rupees did a farmer lose when prices fell 50 per cent
find the price drop when the earlier price and fall per cent are given
compute the new price after a 60 per cent fall in jute prices
what was the money loss per unit when wheat prices halved
convert a percentage price fall into a rupee amount

solution_steps.explain: Multiply the earlier price by the fall percentage and divide by 100 to get the drop in price

concepts.title: Bretton Woods Institutions and Fixed Exchange Rates
concepts.definition: The 1944 Bretton Woods conference created the International Monetary Fund to handle member deficits and the World Bank to finance post-war reconstruction, and pegged national currencies to a dollar that was anchored to gold at 35 dollars per ounce.
concepts.key_idea: The Bretton Woods twins began operations in 1947 under Western industrial control with a US veto, and world trade grew over 8 per cent a year between 1950 and 1970.
question_patterns: what are the bretton woods institutions
what was the purpose of the imf and the world bank
explain the fixed exchange rate system of bretton woods
what was the price of gold fixed under the bretton woods system
why is the dollar called the anchor of the bretton woods system
how were decisions controlled in the imf and world bank

solution_steps.explain: The IMF deals with external surpluses and deficits; the World Bank finances post-war reconstruction and development lending.
Currencies were pegged to the dollar at fixed exchange rates, and the dollar was anchored to gold at 35 dollars per ounce.
Western industrial powers dominated decision-making, with the US holding an effective veto over key decisions.

concepts.title: Gold Value at the Fixed Dollar Price
concepts.definition: Under the Bretton Woods anchor, gold was valued at a fixed 35 dollars per ounce, so the dollar value of any quantity of gold equals the number of ounces multiplied by 35.
concepts.key_idea: This fixed price of 35 dollars an ounce held the dollar to gold and kept world currencies stable until the system collapsed in the 1970s.
question_patterns: calculate the dollar value of a given quantity of gold at the bretton woods price
how many dollars did one ounce of gold cost under bretton woods
find the value in dollars of gold reserves at the fixed price
compute gold value when the ounce quantity is known
what does the fixed gold price of 35 dollars per ounce mean
how was the dollar anchored to gold under bretton woods

solution_steps.action: multiply ounces by the fixed price
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the number of gold ounces by the fixed price of 35 dollars per ounce

concepts.title: Decolonisation, G-77 and the NIEO
concepts.definition: After the Second World War most Asian and African colonies became independent but remained poor and resource-strapped, so developing countries organised as the Group of 77 to demand a New International Economic Order with control over resources and fairer prices.
concepts.key_idea: The Bretton Woods institutions shifted attention to developing countries from the late 1950s, while multinational corporations spread worldwide partly to jump over high import tariffs.
question_patterns: what did the g-77 countries demand through the nieo
why did the bretton woods institutions shift focus to developing countries
what are mncs and why did they spread worldwide
how did decolonisation change the world economy
why did former colonies remain poor after independence
what does a new international economic order mean

solution_steps.explain: Note the two decades after the war in which most Asian and African colonies became free nations.
The group demanded real control over natural resources, more development assistance, fairer raw material prices and better market access.
High import tariffs pushed corporations to set up production inside as many countries as possible, spreading globalisation.
